notes.definition: The efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment, by limiting their movement and controlling the temperature of their surroundings. Some animals are also fed high protein foods to increase growth.
explanation: When an animal eats food, only a small proportion of the energy and biomass in that food becomes new body tissue. Much of the glucose it absorbs is used in respiration, and the energy released is used for movement and to keep the body warm. This energy is transferred to the environment, so it is not available for growth. For farmers, this means much of the food they give their animals does not become meat, eggs or milk.

Farmers can improve the efficiency of food production by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment. One way is to limit the animals' movement, for example by keeping them indoors in pens or cages. Animals that move less use less energy from respiration for movement, so more of the energy from their food can be used for growth. Another way is to control the temperature of their surroundings, for example by keeping them in heated sheds. Animals in warm surroundings transfer less energy to the environment by heating, so they use less energy from respiration to keep warm.

Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth. Protein in the diet provides amino acids that the animal uses to build new tissue such as muscle, so the animals reach a mass suitable for sale more quickly. Methods that combine these ideas, with many animals kept indoors under controlled conditions, are called intensive farming. Intensive farming produces more meat or eggs from the same amount of food, often more cheaply.

Some people have ethical objections to some modern intensive farming methods. They argue that it is cruel to keep animals in small spaces where they cannot move freely or behave naturally, that animal welfare is not respected, and that animals may suffer stress. Crowded conditions also make it easier for diseases to spread, and heating sheds uses energy. Other people argue that intensive methods are needed to produce enough affordable food for a growing population. When you evaluate intensive farming you should give arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion.
keyFacts: Much of the energy from an animal's food is used in respiration for movement and keeping warm, not for growth.
Efficiency of food production can be improved by restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment.
Limiting movement means less energy is used in respiration for movement.
Controlling the temperature of the surroundings means less energy is used to keep warm.
More of the energy from food is then used for growth, so animals gain mass faster.
Some animals are fed high protein foods to increase growth.
These methods are part of intensive farming.
Some people have ethical objections to some modern intensive farming methods.

keyTerms.definition: How much useful food (meat, eggs, milk) is produced compared with the food given to the animals.
Keeping large numbers of animals indoors in controlled conditions, with limited movement and controlled temperature, to increase the efficiency of food production.
The process that releases energy from glucose. Animals use this energy for movement and to keep warm, which reduces the energy left for growth.
Animal feed rich in protein, giving the amino acids needed to build new tissue and increase growth.
A belief that something is morally wrong, for example that keeping animals in small cages is cruel.
The physical and mental wellbeing of animals, including being able to move and behave naturally.

equations.name: Efficiency of transfer to growth
equations.formula: efficiency (%) = energy (or biomass) used for growth ÷ energy (or biomass) in food eaten × 100

workedExamples.title: Efficiency of a pig
workedExamples.question: A pig takes in 100 000 kJ of energy in its food. 35 000 kJ is egested in faeces and 52 000 kJ is used in respiration. The rest is used for growth. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer to growth.

workedExamples.title: Food needed for a target growth
workedExamples.question: Indoor pigs transfer 13% of the biomass in their food into growth. How much food is needed for a pig to gain 65 kg?
steps: 13% of the food mass = 65 kg, so 0.13 × food = 65.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why heating improves efficiency
workedExamples.question: Explain why chickens kept in a warm shed gain mass faster than chickens kept outside in winter, if both eat the same amount of food.
steps: Chickens outside in the cold transfer more energy to the surroundings by heating.
They must use more glucose in respiration to keep their body temperature steady.
Chickens in a warm shed lose less energy to the surroundings, so less of their food is respired to keep warm.
More of the energy and biomass from their food is available for growth.
workedExamples.answer: Less energy is used in respiration to keep warm, so more is available for growth.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think animals kept in warm sheds grow faster because heat makes them grow.
misconceptions.right: In fact warm surroundings reduce the energy the animals transfer to the environment, so less glucose is used in respiration to keep warm and more is available for growth.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say limiting movement means animals 'save energy for later'.
misconceptions.right: In fact less energy is used in respiration for movement, so more of the energy and biomass from food becomes new body tissue now.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think intensive farming creates energy or biomass.
misconceptions.right: In fact it only reduces losses; the animals still cannot transfer more biomass than they eat.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often give only one side when asked to evaluate intensive farming.
misconceptions.right: In fact 'evaluate' needs advantages (more efficient, cheaper food) and disadvantages (ethical objections, disease spread, energy for heating), with a conclusion.

realWorld: Broiler chickens are often reared indoors in heated, lit sheds with limited space, so they reach selling mass in a few weeks.
Pigs in intensive units are kept in pens with controlled temperature and fed high protein feed such as soya meal.
Some consumers choose free-range eggs or meat because of ethical objections to intensive farming, and pay a higher price.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic (improving the efficiency of food production and ethical objections to intensive farming) is in separate Biology (8461) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: Always link the technique to respiration: limiting movement or keeping warm means less energy is used in respiration, so more is used for growth.
Say 'energy is transferred to the environment' rather than 'energy is lost'. Never say energy is 'made' or 'used up'.
For 'evaluate' questions on intensive farming, give at least one advantage and one disadvantage, then a justified conclusion.
Learn the three techniques in the specification: limiting movement, controlling temperature, feeding high protein food.
summary: Much energy from animal food is used in respiration for movement and keeping warm.
Limiting movement reduces energy used for movement.
Controlling surrounding temperature reduces energy used to keep warm.
More energy and biomass from food then go into growth.
Some people have ethical objections to intensive farming methods.

questions.question: Which two methods does a farmer use to restrict energy transfer from food animals to the environment?
options: Feeding them less and letting them roam
Limiting their movement and controlling the temperature of their surroundings
Keeping them outside and giving them more space
Spraying crops with pesticide and using fertiliser
markScheme: 1 mark: limiting their movement and controlling the temperature of their surroundings
questions.explanation: These are the two methods in the specification. Letting animals roam or keeping them outside increases energy transfer to the environment. Pesticides and fertilisers apply to crops, not animals.

questions.question: Why does limiting the movement of farm animals help them grow faster?
options: Less energy is used in respiration for movement, so more is available for growth
The animals eat less food
The animals photosynthesise more
Their muscles stop needing protein
markScheme: 1 mark: less energy is used in respiration for movement, so more is available for growth
questions.explanation: Moving uses energy released by respiration. If animals move less, more of the energy and biomass in their food can become new tissue. Animals do not photosynthesise.

questions.question: Why are some farm animals fed high protein foods?
options: To make them move more
To keep them warm
To reduce the amount of faeces
To increase growth
markScheme: 1 mark: to increase growth
questions.explanation: Protein supplies the amino acids needed to build new tissue such as muscle, so animals grow faster.

questions.question: Chickens are kept in a heated shed. Why does this increase the efficiency of meat production?
options: Heat kills all bacteria in the shed
Heat makes the chickens eat more
Less energy is transferred to the surroundings, so less glucose is respired to keep warm
Warm air contains more oxygen for respiration
markScheme: 1 mark: less energy is transferred to the surroundings, so less glucose is respired to keep warm
questions.explanation: In warm surroundings the chickens lose less energy by heating the environment, so less of their food is respired to maintain body temperature and more is used for growth.

questions.question: Which of these describes intensive farming of animals?
options: Animals kept indoors in pens with controlled temperature
Animals kept on open hillsides all year
Animals allowed to find their own food in woodland
Animals kept outdoors and moved to new fields often
markScheme: 1 mark: animals kept indoors in pens with controlled temperature
questions.explanation: Intensive farming limits movement and controls temperature to reduce energy transfer to the environment. The other options describe extensive or free-range farming.

questions.question: Which of these is an ethical objection to intensive farming?
options: It produces cheaper meat
It increases the efficiency of food production
It uses high protein food
Animals cannot move freely or behave naturally
markScheme: 1 mark: animals cannot move freely or behave naturally
questions.explanation: Ethical objections are about whether something is morally right. Concern for animal welfare is ethical. Cheaper meat and higher efficiency are advantages, and using protein food is a technique.

questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of keeping large numbers of animals close together in an intensive unit?
options: The animals grow more slowly
Diseases can spread more easily between animals
The animals use more energy for movement
The animals transfer more energy to the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: diseases can spread more easily between animals
questions.explanation: Crowding increases contact between animals, so pathogens spread easily. The other options are the opposite of what happens in intensive conditions.

questions.question:
A farmer compares two groups of pigs given the same food. Free-range pigs transfer 9% of the energy in their food to growth; pigs in heated indoor pens transfer 13%.
Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Indoor pigs eat more food than free-range pigs
Free-range pigs produce more meat per kilogram of food
Indoor pigs transfer less energy to the environment, so a larger percentage is used for growth
Indoor pigs respire more than free-range pigs
markScheme: 1 mark: indoor pigs transfer less energy to the environment, so a larger percentage is used for growth
questions.explanation: The food is the same, so the higher efficiency of indoor pigs means less energy was lost through respiration for movement and keeping warm. They produce more meat per kilogram of food, not less.

questions.question: What does 'restricting energy transfer from food animals to the environment' achieve?
options: It increases the total energy in the animals' food
More of the energy from food is used for growth instead of being transferred to the surroundings
It stops the animals from respiring
It allows the animals to digest cellulose more completely
markScheme: 1 mark: more of the energy from food is used for growth
questions.explanation: The food contains the same energy; reducing what is transferred to the environment by movement and heating means more is available for growth. Animals must still respire to stay alive.

questions.question: A farmer wants cattle to gain muscle quickly. Which feed should be added to their diet?
options: High protein pellets
Extra water only
Low protein straw
Salt licks only
markScheme: 1 mark: high protein pellets
questions.explanation: Protein provides amino acids to build muscle. Straw is low in protein, and water and salt do not provide material for growth.

questions.question:
A free-range cow eats 6000 kg of grass in a year and gains 240 kg in mass.
Calculate the efficiency of transfer of biomass from grass to cow.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4%
questions.explanation: Efficiency = biomass gained ÷ biomass eaten × 100 = 240 ÷ 6000 × 100 = 4%.

questions.question:
A pig takes in 100 000 kJ of energy in its food. 35 000 kJ is egested in faeces and 52 000 kJ is used in respiration. The rest is used for growth.
Calculate the percentage of the energy in the food that is used for growth.
questions.explanation: Subtract both losses first to find 13 000 kJ for growth, then 13 000 ÷ 100 000 × 100 = 13%.

questions.question:
When calves were moved into a heated shed, the energy they used in respiration fell from 60 000 kJ to 48 000 kJ per month.
Calculate the percentage decrease in energy used in respiration.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20%
questions.explanation: Decrease = 12 000 kJ. 12 000 ÷ 60 000 × 100 = 20%. Divide by the original value, 60 000.

questions.question:
Pigs in an intensive unit transfer 13% of the biomass in their food into growth.
Calculate the mass of food needed for a pig to gain 65 kg.
markScheme: 1 mark: 500 kg
questions.explanation: Rearrange: food = growth ÷ efficiency = 65 ÷ 0.13 = 500 kg. Check: 13% of 500 = 65 kg.

questions.question:
A calf takes in 120 000 kJ of energy in its food. Outdoors, 4% of this energy is used for growth. In a heated indoor pen, 6% is used for growth.
Calculate how much more energy is used for growth when the calf is kept indoors.
markScheme: 1 mark: outdoors 120 000 × 0.04 = 4800 kJ
1 mark: indoors 120 000 × 0.06 = 7200 kJ
1 mark: difference = 2400 kJ
questions.explanation: 7200 − 4800 = 2400 kJ. A quicker method is 2% of 120 000 = 2400 kJ.

questions.question: Give two ways farmers can restrict energy transfer from food animals to the environment.
markScheme: 1 mark: limit their movement (e.g. keep in small pens)
1 mark: control the temperature of their surroundings (e.g. heated sheds)
questions.explanation: These are the two methods in the specification for reducing energy transfer to the environment.

questions.question: State why some farm animals are given high protein food.
markScheme: 1 mark: to increase growth
questions.explanation: Protein provides amino acids for building new tissue, increasing growth.

questions.question: Explain why keeping animals in small pens increases the efficiency of food production.
markScheme: 1 mark: animals move less, so less energy from respiration is used for movement
1 mark: so more energy / biomass from food is used for growth
questions.explanation: Link the method to respiration and then to growth for both marks.

questions.question: Explain why controlling the temperature of an animal's surroundings increases the efficiency of food production.
markScheme: 1 mark: less energy is transferred to the surroundings / less energy is used to keep warm (less glucose respired)
1 mark: so more energy / biomass from food is used for growth
questions.explanation: Warm surroundings reduce the animal's heat loss, so it needs to respire less glucose to keep its body temperature steady.

questions.question: Give two ethical objections that some people have to modern intensive farming methods.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: animals cannot move freely / kept in small spaces; animals cannot behave naturally; it is cruel / causes stress or suffering; poor animal welfare
questions.explanation: Ethical objections concern animal welfare and whether it is morally right to keep animals in these conditions.

questions.question: Apart from ethical objections, suggest two disadvantages of intensive animal farming.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: diseases spread easily in crowded conditions; heating sheds uses energy / is expensive; regular use of antibiotics may be needed; large amounts of waste can pollute water
questions.explanation: These are practical and environmental problems rather than moral ones, which is what the question asks for.

questions.question: What is meant by intensive farming of animals?
markScheme: 1 mark: keeping (many) animals indoors with limited movement / controlled conditions to increase the efficiency of food production
questions.explanation: Intensive farming controls conditions so that as much food as possible goes into growth.

questions.question: Explain how intensive farming could help improve food security.
markScheme: 1 mark: more of the energy / biomass in animal feed becomes meat or eggs (higher efficiency)
1 mark: so more food is produced from the same resources / food is cheaper and more people can afford it
questions.explanation: Food security means having enough food for a population. Producing more food per kilogram of feed helps feed more people.

questions.question: Name the process in animals that releases energy for movement and is reduced when an animal's movement is limited.
markScheme: 1 mark: respiration
questions.explanation: Respiration releases energy from glucose. Less movement means less energy needed, so less glucose is respired.

questions.question: Explain why feeding cattle high protein food allows the farmer to sell them sooner.
markScheme: 1 mark: protein provides amino acids to build new tissue / muscle
1 mark: so growth increases and cattle reach selling mass more quickly
questions.explanation: High protein feed increases growth, so the animals reach the required mass in less time.

questions.question:
Some chickens are reared for meat in intensive units: heated sheds where each bird has very little space and is fed high protein food.
Evaluate the use of intensive farming to produce chicken meat.
markScheme: Indicative content (advantages):
limited movement means less energy used in respiration for movement
heated sheds mean less energy transferred to surroundings / less used to keep warm
so more energy and biomass from food used for growth: higher efficiency
high protein food increases growth
chickens reach selling mass faster; more meat per kilogram of feed
cheaper meat; helps food security
Indicative content (disadvantages):
ethical objections: birds cannot move freely or behave naturally, poor welfare, stress
disease spreads quickly in crowded sheds
heating uses energy and costs money
Conclusion: a justified judgement, e.g. more efficient but at a cost to animal welfare
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): advantages clearly explained using respiration and energy transfer, disadvantages including ethical objections, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some advantages and disadvantages with some explanation; conclusion may be missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of advantages or disadvantages only.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: An evaluation must weigh both sides. The scientific explanation of the advantage (less energy transferred to the environment, so more for growth) is what lifts an answer into the top level.

questions.question: Describe and explain how farmers can increase the efficiency of meat production from animals.
markScheme: Indicative content:
limit movement (pens, cages, indoors)
so less energy from respiration used for movement
control temperature of surroundings (heated sheds)
so less energy transferred to surroundings / less used to keep warm
more of the energy and biomass from food used for growth
feed high protein food to increase growth
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two methods, each explained in terms of energy for growth.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): methods named with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Each method should be followed by its reason, linking back to more energy or biomass being available for growth.
